soil-hist-119.title: Reading the clocks hidden inside rocks and soil
soil-hist-119.text: Rocks, fossils and sediments carry their own birth certificates, for anyone who can read them. Geochronology is the science of finding their age from signatures held in the materials themselves. Absolute ages come from radioactive isotopes. Radiometric dating measures how far an isotope of known half-life, the time it takes half of it to decay, has decayed. Slowly decaying isotopes reach further back but give less exact ages in years. So {{ref:soil-hist-120}} suits organic samples younger than about 60,000 years, and uranium–lead dating samples older than about 1 million years. Uranium–thorium dating spans a few years to about 700,000 years, on speleothems, the mineral deposits of caves, and on corals, carbonates and fossil bones. Relative ages come from paleomagnetism and stable isotope ratios. Marker horizons, such as dated volcanic ash layers, are so distinctive that their age-equivalence across sites is certain. Incremental methods such as dendrochronology, tree-ring dating, and lichenometry build year-by-year chronologies. Amino acid dating is cheap, but gives no numbers without calibration from other methods at the same site. Combining several indicators, fossils among them, sharpens any age.

soil-hist-120.title: Radiocarbon dating and the clock that starts at death
soil-hist-120.text: Every living thing carries a faint radioactive clock, and death starts it ticking. High in the atmosphere, cosmic rays strike nitrogen and constantly make carbon-14. Plants take it in through photosynthesis, and animals get it from the plants they eat. Radiocarbon dating finds the age of material containing organic carbon from how much carbon-14 is left. Once an organism dies, it stops exchanging carbon and its carbon-14 decays. The half-life is about 5,730 years, so reliable dates reach back roughly 50,000 years. Willard Libby developed the method at the University of Chicago in the late 1940s. It won him the 1960 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Its impact on archaeology was so great that histories of the field call it the 'radiocarbon revolution'. Dates must be corrected for fractionation and reservoir effects. Fossil-fuel burning and the nuclear tests of the 1950s–1960s complicate them further. Small impurities matter: 1% modern carbon makes a 17,000-year-old sample look 600 years younger. Accelerator mass spectrometry counts every carbon-14 atom rather than only decays, so it can date a single seed.

soil-hist-124.title: Luminescence dating: when a grain last saw the sun
soil-hist-124.text: A quartz grain buried in a dune keeps a running tally of radiation. Luminescence dating is a group of methods that find how long ago mineral grains were last exposed to sunlight or strong heating. In buried quartz or feldspar, radiation from cosmic rays and traces of potassium, uranium, thorium and rubidium builds up trapped charge. Light or heat releases it as a glow whose intensity reflects burial time. The age is the equivalent dose, in grays, divided by the environmental dose rate, typically 0.5–5 Gy per 1000 years. The methods assume the grains were 'bleached' at burial: 1–100 s of daylight resets quartz, as usually happens in dunes, loess and some water-laid deposits. Quartz ages typically span 100 to 350,000 years before present, with uncertainties of 5–10% of the age. Feldspar may reach a million years. Needing no organic material, it avoids errors from old, carbon-14-deficient carbon. At Lake Ulaan in Mongolia, wind-blown old carbon made radiocarbon dates up to 5800 years too old. Luminescence was unaffected. {{ref:soil-hist-126}} first dated unheated sediments in 1965, and optical dating followed in 1984.

soil-hist-132.title: Palynology, the science of pollen that refuses to dissolve
soil-hist-132.text: Pollen is tough enough to survive acid baths that dissolve rock minerals. Palynology is the study of acid-resistant microscopic organic remains, such as pollen and spores, found in sediments and sedimentary rocks. These palynomorphs, 5 to 500 micrometers across, also include dinoflagellate cysts, fungi and plant tissue. Laboratories free them from soils, rocks and sediment cores by ultrasonic treatment, wet sieving and acid digestion. Potassium hydroxide removes humic substances, and hydrofluoric acid digests silicate minerals. Acetolysis dissolves the cellulose that hampers work on peat. Quantitative pollen analysis began with Lennart von Post, whose 1916 lecture in Kristiania spread the method. Analysts count each taxon's grains under the microscope and draw a pollen diagram, with depth on the y-axis and abundance on the x-axis. Records from peat or lake sediments reconstruct past vegetation and climate. They also reveal human effects such as logging and land use. Geologists, archaeologists, pedologists and physical geographers all use it, including for dating strata relative to one another.

soil-hist-127.title: Cosmogenic nuclides, atoms forged by rays from space
soil-hist-127.text: Earth's surface sits under a constant, invisible bombardment. When a high-energy cosmic ray strikes an atom's nucleus and knocks out protons and neutrons, it can leave a rare isotope: a cosmogenic nuclide. These form within rocks and soil, in the atmosphere and in meteoroids. The useful ones are absent from the host material when it forms. Their build-up therefore records how long it has been exposed since. Beryllium-10, with a half-life of 1,387,000 years, dates the exposure of rocks, soils and ice cores. Aluminum-26 and chlorine-36 date rocks and sediment. Rock absorbs most of the cosmic-ray flux within its first meter, and that is where new nuclides form. Spallation, the chipping of nuclei by direct hits, dominates in the top 0 to 60 cm. Muon capture takes over a few meters down. Neutron capture depends on snow, soil moisture and trace elements. Altitude matters too: air pressure changes production in minerals by a factor of 30 between sea level and the top of a 5 km mountain.

soil-hist-131.title: δ13C, the carbon signature plants leave in soil
soil-hist-131.text: Plants stamp their soil with a signature of how they photosynthesize. δ13C is a normalized ratio of the stable carbon isotopes carbon-13 and carbon-12. It compares a sample's 13C/12C ratio with a reference standard and reports the difference in parts per thousand, or per mille (‰). The original standard, a Cretaceous belemnite fossil called PDB, ran out and was replaced by standards such as VPDB. Organisms take up light carbon-12 preferentially, so they sit near −25‰, depending on their metabolic pathway. C4 plants, one such pathway group, range from −16 to −10‰; C3 plants run from −33 to −24‰. That gap lets researchers trace the rise of C4 grasses through time. The ratio also separates carbon dioxide from ecosystem respiration from that of burned fossil fuels, the basis of the Suess effect. In a paleosol, carbon isotopes in pedogenic carbonate nodules reconstruct past atmospheric carbon dioxide. On the Loess Plateau, the δ13C of such carbonate rose by 5% over the Late Miocene and Pliocene, a sign of drying.

soil-hist-125.title: Optically stimulated luminescence: grains that glow on cue
soil-hist-125.text: Shine light on an old buried quartz grain and it answers with a faint glow. Optically stimulated luminescence reads a mineral's absorbed radiation dose from that light, to date sediments. Radiation traps electrons at impurities and defects in quartz and feldspar. Light frees them, and they emit light as they recombine at luminescence centers. Grains, usually coarse at 100–200 μm or fine at 4–11 μm, must be extracted without exposure to light. It dates minerals, not organic material, such as the deposition of wind-blown and river sediments. David J. Huntley and colleagues developed it in 1984. Most laboratories now use single-aliquot regeneration (SAR).

soil-hist-135.title: Tephrochronology: volcanic ash as a time marker
soil-hist-135.text: An eruption spreads one moment in time across a whole landscape. Ash falls almost instantly over wide areas. Tephrochronology dates and correlates sequences by their position between layers of volcanic ash, or tephra, of known date. Each eruption leaves a tephra horizon with a unique chemical fingerprint. Once the eruption is dated, that horizon becomes a time marker. It links distant sequences into one 'age-equivalent' chronology and checks other dating methods. Fingerprinting uses the electron microprobe and laser-ablation ICP-MS on single shards, though basaltic tephra chemistry can alter over time. Since the late 1990s, invisible 'cryptotephra' layers have been extracted from peat, lake sediment and loess.

soil-hist-126.title: Thermoluminescence dating and the reset of heat
soil-hist-126.text: Heating a pot in a kiln, or melting rock into lava, sets a clock to zero. Thermoluminescence dating measures the radiation dose crystalline material has gathered since it was last heated, or since sediment last saw sunlight. Heat or sunlight empties its electron traps. Afterwards the surrounding radiation steadily refills them. Heating the sample in the laboratory measures the dose. Dividing it by the yearly dose rate, found from uranium, thorium and potassium contents plus cosmic rays, gives the age. The soil's own dose affects accuracy, so it is ideally measured at the find spot over a long period. Heated objects must have gone above 500 °C. The method serves where radiocarbon dating cannot, as for sediments.

soil-hist-121.title: Radiocarbon calibration: turning lab numbers into calendar dates
soil-hist-121.text: A raw radiocarbon age is not quite a calendar date. The simple decay equation assumes a constant level of atmospheric carbon-14, but that level has varied significantly. Radiocarbon calibration fixes this with a curve of past atmospheric carbon-14, converting a measurement into an estimated calendar age. Tree-ring sequences gave the first calibration data, and Hans Suess published the first curve in 1967. The IntCal curves, first published in 1998 and updated to 2020, come in northern (IntCal20), southern (SHCal20) and marine (MARINE20) versions. Uncalibrated 'conventional radiocarbon ages' still use the Libby half-life of 5568 years. That value was agreed in 1962 to stay consistent with early papers.

soil-hist-122.title: Why soil and peat are hard to radiocarbon date
soil-hist-122.text: Soil mixes young carbon into old, an awkward trait in a clock. Radiocarbon dating of the organic matter in soils and peat is hard to do reliably, because younger humic acid tends to contaminate it. Old carbon from limestone or groundwater can give apparent ages of thousands of years. Humus can do the same or, if younger, lower the apparent age. For soil it is better to sieve out fragments of organic origin and date them with methods that tolerate small samples. In peat, the humins give the most reliable date. They are insoluble in alkali and less contaminated than humic or fulvic acid. Dating soil organic carbon and lake methane showed 0.2 to 2.5 Pg, or petagrams, of permafrost carbon released over the last 60 years.

soil-hist-128.title: Surface exposure dating: how long a rock has seen the sky
soil-hist-128.text: A boulder left by a retreating glacier starts collecting cosmic-ray atoms once exposed. Surface exposure dating estimates how long a rock has been at or near Earth's surface. It dates glacial advances and retreats, erosion history, lava flows, rock slides and fault scarps. It works best for exposures of 10³ to 10⁶ years. Measured concentrations of cosmogenic nuclides, with the cosmic-ray flux and their half-lives, give exposure time, burial time or how fast a drainage basin erodes. Beryllium-10 and aluminum-26 form from the oxygen and silicon in quartz. Their ratio dates burial below the production depth, typically 2–10 meters. Rates are calibrated on samples dated by radiocarbon or luminescence; accelerator mass spectrometry measures the nuclides.

soil-hist-129.title: Beryllium-10, a rain-borne tracer of soil
soil-hist-129.text: Rain delivers a slow clock to the soil surface. Beryllium-10 is a cosmogenic isotope formed in the atmosphere, with a half-life of 1.387 million years, and it traces soil formation and erosion. Beryllium dissolves below about pH 5.5, so rain carries it down. It drops out as the water turns more alkaline, so it accumulates at the soil surface, where its long half-life does not limit how long it stays. It has been used to study soil erosion, soil formation from regolith, the development of lateritic soils and the age of ice cores. Its short-lived relative beryllium-7, with a half-life of 53.22 days, shows that sediments are fresh: less than about 3–4 months old.

soil-hist-123.title: The bomb pulse, a nuclear-age spike in carbon-14
soil-hist-123.text: Above-ground nuclear tests almost doubled the relative concentration of carbon-14 in the atmosphere. That sudden rise, from the first tests in 1945 until the 1963 Limited Test Ban Treaty, is the bomb pulse. Since the ban the excess has fallen by about 4% a year. That steady decline lets scientists date recent tissues and deaths. The pulse has also tested atmospheric transport models and tracked carbon moving between the atmosphere and oceanic or terrestrial sinks. If no more nuclear weapons are detonated above ground, it will die out around 2030.

soil-hist-130.title: Lead-210 dating, a century of soil movement
soil-hist-130.text: A fine, steady fallout from the sky settles on soils all over the world. It comes from the decay products of radon-222 gas. Among them is lead-210, a radioactive isotope in the uranium-238 decay chain with a half-life of 22.20 years. Excess lead-210 from this fallout builds up in surface soils. Its activity profile with depth reconstructs soil redistribution over the past century. That gives erosion and deposition rates and tests conservation practices. Its deposition is continuous and global, so it complements the medium-term record from human-made radionuclides such as caesium-137. It suits sedimentation chronologies on time scales shorter than 100 years.

soil-hist-133.title: Rhizoliths, the fossil ghosts of roots
soil-hist-133.text: Roots rot away, but the shapes they leave in soil can outlast them. A rhizolith is an organosedimentary structure formed by plant roots in soils or paleosols. The family includes root molds, casts, tubules, petrifactions and rhizocretions. Some roots secrete bicarbonate rather than hydrogen ions, raising the surrounding pH. Calcium carbonate may then precipitate around them as rhizocretions. Rhizohaloes are gray reduced zones with reddish rims around decayed roots. Rhizolith mineralogy shows how waterlogged a paleosol was. They help identify paleosols, but only in post-Silurian beds, since plants with extensive roots did not flourish before then.

soil-hist-134.title: When roots first broke rock into soil
soil-hist-134.text: Earlier non-vascular plants lacked the deep roots needed to break solid rock into regolith and soil. The Silurian-Devonian Terrestrial Revolution was the rapid spread and diversification of land plants and fungi between 428 and 359 million years ago. The new roots eroded rock and built the pedosphere, a water-holding layer rich in minerals and organic matter. With their microbial partners they formed the rhizosphere, which sped weathering and released phosphates, calcium and magnesium, as pedogenic carbonates show. Enhanced silicate weathering is thought to have cut atmospheric CO2 from around 6300 to 2100 ppmv. Researchers still disagree, though. Another view holds that plants slowed weathering and lowered CO2 mainly by burying organic carbon in wetlands.

openers.paleopedology-and-soil-dating: A grain of quartz can record the last time it saw daylight. Buried soils, sediments and rocks hold many such clocks, and this chapter is about reading them. Some count the carbon-14 left in organic matter. Others read the radiation dose stored in mineral grains, or the rare isotopes cosmic rays make in rock at the surface. Layers of volcanic ash, microscopic pollen and spores, and carbon isotope ratios add markers of their own, and every clock has its quirks, from shifting atmospheric carbon-14 to young humic acid that contaminates old soil and peat.

reviews.paleopedology-and-soil-dating: Every clock in this chapter reads a signature locked inside the material itself. Carbon-14 dates organic matter back about 50,000 years, once calibrated against past atmospheric levels and cleaned of the younger humic acid that troubles soil and peat. Mineral grains count the radiation dose since sunlight or heat last emptied them, cosmogenic nuclides record how long rock and soil have lain exposed, and lead-210 and the bomb pulse time the last century. Volcanic ash layers, pollen diagrams and the δ13C of soil carbonates add markers and past climates. Together they reach back to the roots that first broke rock into soil between 428 and 359 million years ago.
